headline: Phone Call Script: First Sentences to Read When You Dial
sub: It only has to get you through the first fifteen seconds, and you can read it.
items: A problem with an order: Hi, I have a problem with my account and I'm hoping you can help me sort it out. Can I explain what happened?
Booking an appointment: Hi, I'd like to book an appointment. Are you the right person for that?
Canceling: Hi, I'd like to cancel. Can you tell me what you need from me to do that?
Making a complaint: Hi, I'd like to make a complaint. Can you tell me how that works here, and who I need to speak to?
proof: It only has to get you through the first fifteen seconds, and you can read it.

headline: Phone Call Anxiety: A Four-Rung Ladder From the Page to the Call
sub: Coaches often suggest working up from easier calls. It's worth trying, not proven, and you can skip any rung.
items: Rung 1: the page. Write the five things. Stop there if you need to.
Rung 2: no one to answer. Call after hours and leave the voicemail, or listen to the recorded greeting.
Rung 3: an easy call. Ask something with no stakes, like opening hours or whether they can help with your kind of problem.
Rung 4: the call. Dial with the page in front of you and read the first sentence.

headline: Wrong Charge on Your Bill: Four Opening Lines for the Phone
sub: Each opens with the problem, not an apology, and ends with a question.
items: Wrong amount charged: Hi, the amount I've been charged isn't what I was expecting. Can you tell me what it's for?
Charged twice: Hi, I've been charged twice for the same thing and I'd like to get it put right. Can you look at the account for me?
Charged after canceling: Hi, I canceled this and I've been charged since. Can you check when the cancellation was recorded?
Charge you don't recognize: Hi, there's a charge on my account I don't recognize. Can you tell me what it is?
proof: Each opens with the problem, not an apology, and ends with a question.

headline: How a Customer Service Call Goes: Open, Facts, Ask, Read Back, Close
sub: Say what happened, once, in order.
items: Open: Hi, I'm waiting on a refund that hasn't arrived. Can you tell me whether it's been sent, and when?
Facts, once: Your colleague Dana said it would take five business days on the 9th.
The ask: I'd like the refund sent today, or a date I can rely on.
Read back: So the refund goes out by Friday. Can I have a reference number for this call?
Close: And your name, please? Thank you.
proof: Say what happened, once, in order

headline: What to Say When Customer Service Says They Can't Help
sub: Polite and specific works better than firm.
items: They say they can't help: I understand that's the policy. What options do I have from here?
Asking for a supervisor: Is there someone with more authority to change this that I can speak to? I'll hold.
You're told to call back: Can you note on the account that I called today and what I asked for? Then I'll say so when I call again.

headline: How to Say No on the Phone: When They Push Back, Repeat It in Fewer Words
sub: If they push, repeat your answer in fewer words rather than defending it in more.
items: They push back: I understand it's disappointing. I've thought about it and my answer is still no.
They ask why: I'd rather not go into all of it. It's just not something I can do this time.
You need a moment: Can I have a minute to think about that? I'd like to call you back tonight.
proof: If they push, repeat your answer in fewer words rather than defending it in more.

headline: How Long to Wait Before Following Up on an Email: A Chase Plan
sub: The days are a suggestion we'd use for something that isn't an emergency.
items: Day 0: you send. Note the date, who it went to, and what you asked for.
Day 5: nothing yet. Chase by a different route, such as a call if you emailed. Ask for a date.
Day 10: still nothing. Write again to the same person and add a second person or a general address.
Day 15: still nothing. Decide whether it needs escalating, or whether you can let it go.
proof: The days are a suggestion we'd use for something that isn't an emergency.

headline: Follow Up Email Wording: Ask for a Date, Not an Update
sub: Ask for a date rather than an update, because an update can be nothing.
items: A decision: Hello, I'm following up because I need to know either way. When do you think you'll be able to tell me?
Money owed to you: Hello, I'm following up because it's still outstanding. Can you tell me when it will be dealt with?
A document or form: Hello, I'm still waiting on this. Could you tell me when I can expect it, or what you need from me first?
proof: Ask for a date rather than an update, because an update can be nothing.
